tema: What It Was Like to Get Surgery Before Anesthesia
titulo: What It Was Like to Get Surgery Before Anesthesia
descricao:
London, 1840. The best surgeon in the city can cut off your leg in under three minutes. You will be awake for all of them.

Mr. Squarington takes you through one day as a patient before anesthesia: the brandy, the leather strap, the operating theatre full of spectators, the surgeon in a coat stiff with old blood, the infection that came after, and the day in 1846 when everything changed.

All true. All documented. Unfortunately.

Would you have survived the operation, or the week after? Tell us in the comments.

falas: London, 1840. The best surgeon in the city is famous for one thing.
He can cut off your leg in under three minutes.
|You will be awake for all of them.
Good evening, round-headed citizens.
Today, you are a patient. Before anesthesia.
No gas. No injection. No count backwards from ten.
Just you, a table, and a man with a saw.
|Let's begin your day.
Seven in the morning. Your big day.
You wake up in a tiny room. Your leg is infected. It smells. It has smelled for weeks.
The doctor has made his decision. The leg has to go.
|You'd like a second opinion. The second opinion is also a saw.
So you prepare the only way people could.
A glass of brandy. Then another.
If you're lucky, a few drops of laudanum. That's opium, dissolved in alcohol.
It does not stop the pain. It just makes you care slightly less about it.
|Slightly.
Nine o'clock. You arrive at the hospital.
In 1840, hospitals were not where rich people went to get better.
Rich people were operated on at home. On the kitchen table.
Hospitals were for the poor. And you are very poor.
The ward smells of rot, sweat and old blood.
Nobody has washed their hands. Nobody thinks they need to.
Germs? Nobody believes in germs yet. Doctors think disease comes from bad air.
|They are half right. The air is terrible.
Ten o'clock. Now, you wait.
Operations happen around midday. Not for your comfort. For the light.
The theatre has a big glass roof, and the surgeon needs the sun to see what he's cutting.
|So if it's a cloudy day in London... good luck.
From the ward, you can hear the patient before you. Through the wall.
Some patients panicked and tried to escape. They did not get far. Remember the infected leg?
|Running was not an option. Hopping was not much better.
Meanwhile, the surgeon lays out his tools.
A knife. A saw. A hook. And a tourniquet, to squeeze the leg and slow the bleeding.
The handles are beautiful. Carved wood. Ivory. Little grooves everywhere.
|Perfect for collecting yesterday's patient.
Students paid fees to watch all of this. It was the best seat in medical school.
Eleven o'clock. They call your name.
You are carried into the operating theatre. And yes, it's called a theatre for a reason.
Around the table, rows of wooden benches go up to the ceiling. They are full.
Medical students. Curious gentlemen. People who simply had a free morning.
|You are the show.
Under the table, there's a box of sawdust. It's there to soak up the blood.
Then the surgeon walks in.
He's wearing his operating coat. It used to be black. Now it's brown, stiff and cracking.
That's dried blood, from years of operations. A dirty coat meant a busy surgeon.
Surgeons were proud of it.
|You are not proud of it.
Four strong men grab your arms and legs. They're called dressers.
Their job is to hold you down. No matter what.
Someone puts a leather strap between your teeth. Bite this.
|That's the anesthesia.
Eleven oh two.
The most famous surgeon in London was Robert Liston. Tall, strong, and incredibly fast.
He often held the bloody knife between his teeth, so both hands were free for the saw.
Speed was everything. The faster the cut, the less you suffered, and the less blood you lost.
The story goes that he'd shout to the crowd: time me, gentlemen.
And they did. Pocket watches came out all around the room.
|I would also be timing it. From very far away.
The knife goes in. Then the saw.
You scream. Everyone expected you to scream. Screaming was normal.
Liston could take off a leg in about two and a half minutes.
There's even a legend that once, in his hurry, he took off his assistant's fingers too.
Most historians think that story is made up.
|But nobody in that room would have been surprised.
Two and a half minutes later, it's over. The leg is gone. You're still here.
|Congratulations. That was the easy part.
Now the surgeon has to stop the bleeding. He ties each artery shut with a silk thread.
Then he leaves the long ends of the thread hanging out of the wound.
|On purpose.
The idea was that after a few days, the thread would rot, and could be pulled out.
|Rot. On purpose. Inside you.
And honestly? That was progress.
Three hundred years earlier, gunshot wounds were treated with boiling oil.
Until 1537, when a French army surgeon, Ambroise Paré, ran out of oil in the middle of a battle.
He used a cheap mix of egg yolk, rose oil and turpentine instead. And he couldn't sleep, sure his patients would die.
The next morning, they were doing better than the ones he had boiled.
|Medicine, ladies and gentlemen. Sometimes progress is just running out of oil.
The next week.
In 1840, the operation wasn't the real killer. What came after was.
Nobody cleaned the instruments. The same knife moved from patient to patient.
Sometimes, it was wiped. On the coat.
The wound gets red. Then hot. Then it starts to smell.
Doctors called the yellow stuff coming out laudable pus. They thought it was a good sign.
|It was not a good sign.
Decades later, a Scottish doctor counted the dead. In big city hospitals, about four in ten amputation patients didn't survive.
Rich patients, at home, on their kitchen tables, did much better.
|Being poor was basically a medical condition.
And if you think this only happened to poor men, let me tell you about Fanny Burney.
Fanny Burney was a famous English novelist.
In 1811, in Paris, her doctors decided she needed surgery on her breast.
Her surgeon was Dominique Larrey. The chief surgeon of Napoleon's army.
She was awake. They put a thin handkerchief over her face.
She could see the knife through it.
The operation took about twenty minutes.
She later wrote that she screamed the entire time, and that for months she could not even talk about it.
She survived. And months later, she wrote down every second of it in a letter to her sister.
That letter still exists. Historians still read it today.
|She lived another twenty-nine years. Tougher than all of us.
Then came 1846.
A year earlier, another dentist, Horace Wells, tried laughing gas in front of a room full of Harvard students.
Halfway through, the patient groaned. The crowd shouted humbug, and Wells was laughed out of the room.
|Laughing gas. Everyone laughed. Except Wells.
In Boston, a dentist named William Morton tried something new. Ether.
Ether was already famous. At parties, people sniffed it for fun.
They called them ether frolics.
On October sixteenth, in front of a crowd of doctors, Morton put a patient to sleep.
And a surgeon removed a tumour from his neck.
The patient woke up and said he had felt no pain.
The room went silent.
|A room full of surgeons. Speechless. Imagine that.
Two months later, the news reached London. And who did the first operation under ether in Britain?
Robert Liston. The fastest knife in London.
He took off a leg in about half a minute.
The patient woke up and asked when they were going to start.
|Same speed. Zero screaming.
Liston turned to the students and said: this Yankee dodge, gentlemen, beats mesmerism hollow.
In 1847, a Scottish doctor started using chloroform. A few years later, even Queen Victoria used it to give birth.
|If it's good enough for the Queen, it's good enough for your leg.
A few decades later, Joseph Lister started cleaning wounds with carbolic acid.
And surgery finally stopped being a death sentence.
So next time you're nervous at the dentist, remember.
Nobody is going to hold you down. Nobody is going to time you.
|And nobody is wearing a coat made of other people.
Goodnight, round-headed citizens.
|Wash your hands.
